📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We boosted load_dataset('dataset', streaming=True), streaming datasets without downloading them with one line of code!

Start training on multi-TB datasets immediately, without complex setups, downloading, no "disk out of space", or 429 “stop requesting!” errors.It's super fast! Outrunning our local SSDs when training on 64xH100 with 256 workers downloading data. We've improved streaming to have 100x fewer requests, → 10× faster data resolution → 2x sample/sec, → 0 worker crashes at 256 concurrent workers.

Recent findings suggest that loading data, especially at the terabyte scale, is a major pain in any machine learning workflow. We suffered this while training SmolLM3, at one point we had to wait 3 hours before each run to download enough data.

Sources indicate that streaming has always been possible in the datasets library, but large scale training with massive datasets remained a challenge. That changes today 🔥. We spent a few months improving the backend, focusing on streaming datasets to make it faster and more efficient.

First things first: our changes are backwards compatible. You can still stream any dataset from the Hub with the same simple streaming=True flag. It's as easy as ever. 🚀.

Thousands of AI developers around the world use datasets daily; they should just get improved performance with zero extra work.

Streaming was a lifesaver to quickly understand a dataset, but to train models, people were usually downloading the data locally, or using a cloud storage service such as S3. That's what we were doing for training SmolVLM, we had all of our data on S3 and were streaming directly from it.

We wanted to change that, so we decided to use streaming from the Hub when we were developing nanoVLM. Soon we found a big matter: our test run generated over 100,000 requests in under a minute, which got our IP blocked by the Hub! 😅 This happened because every DataLoader worker was initializing the dataset independently. As we dug deeper, we found that this creates a storm of redundant requests, many of which are unnecessary. Our changes ultimately reduced startup requests by a factor of 100. In total, our improvements delivered:.

In a recent development, so, what changed? We focused on two phases: startup and streaming.

1. Startup⚡️ The initial resolution of data files was creating a ton of requests. We made two major changes:.

In a recent development, 2. Streaming 🏎️ To improve throughput during streaming itself, we've introduced two fresh features:.

This is how we can increase the minimum request size when streaming from 32MiB (default) to 128MiB and configure prefetching:.

Together, these improvements can double your data throughput, allowing you to train faster and more efficiently.

It has been revealed that hugging Face uses Xet: a dedupe-based storage which enables fast deduped uploads and downloads. Unlike traditional remote storage, data transfers are faster on Xet because duplicated data is only transferred once. For example: uploading a large scale dataset to Hugging Face leverages Xet which accelerates uploads. Once the dataset is uploaded, it can be streamed right away.

It has been revealed that deduplication for Parquet is enabled through Parquet Content Defined Chunking (CDC). Thanks to Parquet CDC and Xet deduplication, uploading datasets on Hugging Face is faster than on any traditional remote storage.

This is supported by our pyspark_huggingface package, a Spark Data Source to read/write HF datasets. It includes Parquet CDC and Xet support, accelerating data transfers on HF dramatically.

In a recent development, some data file formats are not supported in datasets, and sometimes there is a need for more control, so we made it easy to build custom streaming pipelines. This has been battle-tested in the LeRobot library to sample video frames, and in the WebDataset library to stream TAR archives.

We improved the HfFileSystem in the huggingface_hub library to efficiently read files from remote Hugging Face dataset repositories and stream data:.

Passing a HfFileSystem to a torch DataLoader reuses the cached results from .ls() and .glob() which eliminates the need for additional requests when listing data files.

In a recent development, we're now using these streaming enhancements in nanoVLM to train the next generation of SmolVLMs. With these tweaks, we achieve better performance from streaming than from training on our cluster's hierarchical hard disk setup. In fact, streaming is now as fast as reading the data from local SSDs! Previously, transferring data to local SSDs was the process that used to delay our trainings by three-hours. For more details, check out our GitHub.

These powerful new features landed in the datasets and huggingface_hub libraries. To take advantage of them, simply upgrade your libraries and check out the documentation:.

According to recent reports, to celebrate this, we preconcatenated and shuffled all the data sources in FineVision into FineVisionMax. You can use this single combined dataset to train your VLM – no need to handle multiple datasets manually!

And you can see how we do it at scale in nanoVLM!

Chiral gapped states are universally non-topological

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (178 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2510.23720v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose an operator generalization of the Li-Haldane conjecture regarding the entanglement Hamiltonian of a disk in a 2+1D chiral gapped groundstate. The logic applies to regions with sharp corners, from which we derive several universal properties regarding corner entanglement. These universal properties follow from a set of locally-checkable conditions on the wavefunction. We also define a quantity $(\mathfrak{c}_{\text{tot}})_{\text{min}}$ that reflects the robustness of corner entanglement contributions, and show that it provides an obstruction to a gapped boundary. One reward from our analysis is that we can construct a local gapped Hamiltonian within the same chiral gapped phase from a given wavefunction; we conjecture that it is closer to the low-energy renormalization group fixed point than the original parent Hamiltonian. Our analysis of corner entanglement reveals the emergence of a universal conformal geometry encoded in the entanglement structure of bulk regions of chiral gapped states that is not visible in topological field theory. Our formalism also gives an explanation of the modular commutator formula for the chiral central charge.

#61864. Industry News: Voice Cloning with Consent

📅 28 Oct 2025 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1433 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Voice Cloning with Consent

📅 28 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1433 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in this blog post, we introduce the idea of a 'voice consent gate' to support voice cloning with consent.
  • According to recent reports, realistic voice generation technology has gotten uncannily good in the past few years.
  • Voice generation, and in particular the subtask of voice cloning, has notable risks and benefits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in this blog post, we introduce the idea of a 'voice consent gate' to support voice cloning with consent. We provide an example Space and accompanying code to start the ball rolling on the idea.

According to recent reports, realistic voice generation technology has gotten uncannily good in the past few years. In some situations, it’s possible to generate a synthetic voice that sounds almost exactly like the voice of a real person. And today, what once felt like science fiction is reality: Voice cloning. With just a few seconds of recorded speech, anyone’s voice can be made to say almost anything.

Voice generation, and in particular the subtask of voice cloning, has notable risks and benefits. The risks of “deepfakes”, such as the cloned voice of former President Biden used in robocalls, can mislead people into thinking that people have stated things that they haven’t said. On the other hand, voice cloning can be a powerful beneficial tool, helping people who’ve lost the ability to speak communicate in their own voice again, or assisting people in learning upcoming languages and dialects.

So how do we create meaningful use without malicious use? We’re exploring one possible answer: a voice consent gate. That’s a system where a voice can be cloned only when the speaker explicitly indicates they consent. In other words, the model won’t speak in your voice unless you say it’s okay.

We provide a basic demo of this idea below:.

Sources indicate that the voice consent gate is a piece of infrastructure we're exploring that provides methods for ethical principles like consent to be embedded directly into AI system workflows. In our demo, this means the model only starts once the speaker’s consent phrase has been both spoken and recognized, effectively making consent a prerequisite for action. This turns an abstract principle into a concrete system condition, creating a traceable, auditable interaction: an AI model can only run after an unambiguous act of consent.

Sources indicate that such design choices matter beyond voice cloning. They illustrate how AI systems can be built to respect autonomy by default, and how transparency and consent can be made functional, not just declarative.

To create a basic voice cloning system with a voice consent gate, you need three parts:.

Our observation: Since some voice-cloning systems can now generate speech similar to a speaker’s voice using just one sentence, a sentence used for consent can also be used for voice cloning.

According to recent reports, the consent bit: To create a voice consent gate in an English voice cloning system, generate a short, natural-sounding English utterance (~20 words) for a person to read aloud that clearly states their informed consent in the current context. We recommend explicitly including a consent phrase and the model name, such as “I give my consent to use the < MODEL > voice cloning model with my voice”. We also recommend using an audio recording that cannot be uploaded, but that instead comes directly from a microphone, to make sure that the sentence isn’t part of an earlier recording that’s been manipulated. Pairing this with a novel (previously unsaid) sentence further helps to directly index the current consent context - supporting explicit, active, context-specific, informed consent. While this design reduces risks of reusing prior recordings, it’s not foolproof; a person could still generate a matching phrase using another TTS system. Future iterations could explore lightweight audio provenance checks, speaker-embedding similarity, or metadata from real-time capture to help verify that the consent audio originates from the intended speaker.

The suitable-for-voice-cloning bit: Previous work on voice cloning has shown that the phrases provided by the speaker must have phonetic variety, covering diverse vowels and consonants; have a “neutral” or polite tone, without background noise and with the speaker in a comfortable position; and have a clear start and end (i.e., don’t trim the clip mid-word).

It has been revealed that to enact both of these aspects within the demo, we prompt a language model to create pairs of sentences: one expressing explicit consent, and another neutral sentence that adds phonetic diversity (covering different vowels, consonants, and tones). Each prompt utilizes a randomly-chosen everyday topic (like the weather, food, or music) to keep the sentences varied and comfortable to say, aiding in creating recordings that are clear, natural, and phonetically rich, while also containing an unambiguous statement of consent. This generation step is automated rather than pre-written so that each user receives a unique sentence pair, preventing reuse of the same text and ensuring that consent recordings are specific to the current session. In other words, the language model generates two fresh sentences per consent instance: one for explicit consent and one for phonetic variety. For example, the language model might generate: “I give my consent to use my voice for generating audio with the model EchoVoice. The weather is bright and calm this morning.” This approach ensures that every sample used for cloning contains verifiable, explicit consent, while remaining suitable as technical input for high-quality voice synthesis. (Note: It's not required that the language model be a "large" language model, which brings its own consent complications.).

Once the speaker’s input matches the generated text, the voice cloning system can start, using the speaker’s consent audio as the input.

Industry observers note that there are a few options for doing this, and we’d love to hear further ideas. For now, there’s:.

You can copy the code to suit your own use.

The code is modular so it can be sliced and diced in different ways to incorporate into your own projects. We’ll be working on making this more robust and secure over time, and we’re curious to hear your ideas on how to improve.

Handled responsibly, this technology doesn’t have to haunt us. It can instead become a respectful collaboration between humans and machines — no ghosts in the machine, just good practice. 🎃.

Not a big fan of trying to legislate every problem away but if malicious deep fakes are already illegal in most jurisdictions it seems that malicious voice cloning ought to be too.

I think the problem with enforcement will be offshore usage (i.e. if a person from country X is illegally using a voice clone of a person from country Y, how will enforcement work?), as has already been shown with widespread global IP misuse. The second concern is going to be detection. Who is going to check that every single AI voice was or was not cloned with consent? Anything that would truly prevent misuse with robust checks would probably stifle the ability to iterate and develop quickly and anything that didn't stifle the ability to iterate and develop quickly probably wouldn't truly prevent misuse. The classic regulatory Catch-22.

It's problems like these that kind of necessitate a global response and whilst I'm usually not one to advocate for supranational law-making, it would be nice to see the so-called international community create a joint response or at least initiative on this topic because it's going to be a brutal wake-up call one day.

Sources indicate that at this point even just outreach and education on this topic would be helpful. In my time working with random developers and others in the OSS community, I've come across several suspicious requests from people I hardly know asking me for seemingly random recordings of my voice. Someone who doesn't understand the potential for misuse might provide such a recording and inadvertently have their voice used in scam campaigns.

In a recent development, I have tested it in local... its wonderful... We have to extend it to all the languages.

Sources indicate that @ZennyKenny 's point about suspicious voice recording requests hits home. We're living in an era where 'Can you say something for my ringtone?' has become the new 'Can I borrow your SSN for a second?' The consent gate approach at least makes the ask more obvious: 'Hey, can you explicitly consent to me cloning your voice while reading this phonetically diverse sentence about coffee?' Much harder to slip that one past someone!

I saw your project and found it very interesting. I tried to contribute to it by adding a multilingual support and local sentence generation (with ollama and llama3:8b) and voice cloning using XTTS v2. I uploaded the code on GitHub, you can find it here: https://github.com/faridgnank02/voice-cloning.

Please let me know how you feel about it.

Very interesting! But couldn't the consent by bypassed using another voice cloning model that doesn't require verification? E.g. use that to generate the verification audio.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Optimal Quantum Sensing Algorithms for Discrete-Frequency Spectroscopy

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (227 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21560v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Spectroscopy is a versatile tool that drives scientific discovery and underpins modern technologies. Quantum sensing offers promising opportunities to advance spectroscopy through enhanced sensitivity and spectral and spatial resolution. However, existing approaches largely focus on improving general measurement capabilities, often overlooking the structure of specific sensing tasks and leaving potential performance gains untapped. Here, we develop an algorithmic approach to quantum sensing tailored to various spectroscopic tasks, providing latest avenues for improvement. Specifically, we consider general time-varying signals supported on a known set of $N$ candidate frequencies, a setting we call discrete-frequency spectroscopy. We formulate three types of practically motivated sensing tasks---Detection, Search, and Learning---that require progressively more spectral information. For all tasks, we design optimal quantum sensing algorithms achieving a $\sqrt{N}$ speedup over conventional frequency-scanning approaches. Optimal Detection and Search need only a single-qubit sensor under $\pi$-pulse control, whereas optimal Learning provably requires coherent processing with a quantum computer. End-to-end numerical simulations incorporating various experimental imperfections predict up to two-orders-of-magnitude speedup in Detection. As an example, we analyze the feasibility of our Detection and Search algorithms for real-world molecular screening based on state-of-the-art nitrogen-vacancy centers. We also show how quantum-computing-enhanced Learning enables wireless communication in a weak-signal regime where conventional methods fail. Our results establish a practical route toward realizing quantum advantages via designing task-specific sensing algorithms.

#61858. What kind of quantum advantage is this?

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (183 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

What kind of quantum advantage is this?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (183 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.21239v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum advantage encompasses fundamentally different claims, from resource reductions to exponential separations in sample complexity. Evaluating these claims requires distinguishing how an algorithm achieves an advantage from what is necessary for the separation and how strongly it is supported against classical alternatives. We propose a multi-label taxonomy that makes these distinctions explicit, classifying structural, interference, and coherent mechanisms while separately recording their necessity and the evidence for the classical comparison. Coherent mechanisms are further divided into memory and output, reflecting distinct restrictions on quantum information processing. A two-part entanglement-breaking test distinguishes loss of information from loss of algorithmic efficiency. The hidden subgroup problem illustrates the distinction: among the cases examined, cross-copy coherence is information-theoretically necessary only for the symmetric group. We present this as a diagnostic methodology rather than a theory of quantum advantage: for a new claim, it identifies the relevant adversary, separates the mechanisms a protocol uses from those shown to be necessary, and records the strength of the evidence and the quality of the advantage separately.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we are excited to share Granite 4.0 Nano, our smallest models yet, released as part of IBM's Granite 4.0 model family. Designed for the edge and on-device applications, these models demonstrate excellent performance for their size and represent IBM's continued commitment to develop powerful, useful, models that don't require hundreds of billions of parameters to get the job done.

Sources indicate that like all Granite 4.0 models, the Nano models are released under an Apache 2.0 license with native architecture support on popular runtimes like vLLM, llama.cpp, and MLX. The models were trained with the same improved training methodologies, pipelines, and over 15T tokens of training data developed for the original Granite 4.0 models. This release includes variants benefiting from the Granite 4.0’s new, efficient hybrid architecture, and like all Granite language models, the Granite 4.0 Nano models also carry with them IBM's ISO 42001 certification for responsible model development, giving users added confidence that models are built and governed to global standards.

Specifically, Granite 4.0 Nano comprises of 4 instruct models and their base model counterparts:.

Building sub-billion to ~1 billion parameter models is an active and competitive space, with advancements in performance and architectures recently made by a number of model developers such as Alibaba (Qwen), LiquidAI (LFM), Google (Gemma) and others. When compared to these other models, Granite 4.0 Nano models demonstrate a significant increase in capabilities that can be achieved with a minimal parameter footprint, as measured by a series of general benchmarks across General Knowledge, Math, Code, and Safety domains.

In a recent development, chart 1. Average accuracy of 0.2B–2B parameter models across Knowledge, Math, Code, and Safety benchmarks. See Appendix I for full details.

In addition to more general benchmarks, Granite Nano models outperformed several similarly sized models on tasks critical for agentic workflows, including instruction following and tool calling, as measured by IFEval and Berkley's Function Calling Leaderboard v3 (BFCLv3) benchmarks.

Industry observers note that chart 2. Accuracy on IFEval and BFCLv3 benchmarks.

Full details of the Granite 4.0 Nano can be found on the Hugging Face model cards. Moving forward, expect to see more releases from IBM as we continue to grow the Granite 4.0 family and work to make AI a more efficient and effective tool for developers.

In a recent development, appendix I. Breakdown of General Performance Benchmarks.

We just tested local granite-4-h-tiny model for contract analysis in Word: https://youtu.be/acX1CqF8TDA.

Recent findings suggest that it's impressive. We proposal to give nano a try soon.

In a recent development, the whole Granite series is underrated. I've been training the Granite 3 and 4 small models and they learn very swiftly. They're my go-to models for specialized tasks.

Industry News: Relaxing the i.i.d. state preparation assumption with the block QKD protocol

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (124 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.21048v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this work, we propose a novel approach to handling the independent and identically distributed assumption for the state preparation in prepare-and measure QKD protocols. Contrary to previous approaches, we do not prove the security using sub-protocols, and instead opt to guarantee security in the presence of correlations by dividing the communication into finite blocks of consecutive pulses, and adding an additional assumption of no dependence between each block. In turn we obtain a protocol which uses only a relaxed i.i.d. assumption and is easier to implement than subprotocol-style approaches since it does not require separate statistics for each sub-protocol, whose number grows with the correlation length of the underlying dependency.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, simulation has been a cornerstone in medical imaging to address the data gap. However, in healthcare robotics until now, it's often been too slow, siloed, or difficult to translate into real-world systems. That’s now changing. With upcoming advances in GPU-accelerated simulation and digital twins, developers can design, test, and validate robotic workflows entirely in virtual environments - reducing prototyping time from months to days, improving model accuracy, and enabling safer, faster innovation before a single device reaches the operating room.

That's why NVIDIA introduced Isaac for Healthcare earlier this year, a developer framework for AI healthcare robotics, that enables developers in solving these challenges via integrated data collection, training, and evaluation pipelines that work across both simulation and hardware. Specifically, the Isaac for Healthcare v0.4 release provides people with an end-to-end SO-ARM based starter workflow and the bring your own operating room tutorial. The SO-ARM starter workflow lowers the barrier for MedTech developers to experience the full workflow from simulation to training to deployment and start building and validating autonomously on real hardware right away.

In this post, we'll walk through the starter workflow and its technical implementation details to help you build a surgical assistant robot in less time than ever imaginable before.

The SO-ARM starter workflow introduces a fresh way to explore surgical assistance tasks, and provides developers with a complete end-to-end pipeline for autonomous surgical assistance:.

This workflow gives developers a safe, repeatable environment to train and refine assistive skills before moving into the Operating Room.

The workflow implements a three-stage pipeline that integrates simulation and real hardware:.

Notably, over 93% of the data used for policy training was generated synthetically in simulation, underscoring the strength of simulation in bridging the robotic data gap.

Sources indicate that the workflow combines simulation and real-world data to address the fundamental challenge that training robots in the real world is expensive and limited, while pure simulation often fails to capture real-world complexities. The approach uses approximately 70 simulation episodes for diverse scenarios and environmental variations, combined with 10-20 real-world episodes for authenticity and grounding. This mixed training creates policies that generalize beyond either domain alone.

Notably, developers could run all the simulation, training and deployment (3 computers needed for physical AI) on one DGX Spark.

After collecting both simulation and real-world data, convert and combine datasets for training:.

In a recent development, the trained model processes natural language instructions such as "Prepare the scalpel for the surgeon" or "Hand me the forceps" and executes the corresponding robotic actions. With the latest LeRobot release (v0.4.0) you will be able to post-train GR00T N1.5 natively in LeRobot!

Industry observers note that simulation is most powerful when it's part of a loop: collect data → train → evaluate → deploy. Isaac Lab supports this full pipeline:.

This reduces time from experiment to deployment and makes sim-to-real a practical part of daily development.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A hands-on guide to collecting data, training policies, and deploying autonomous medical robotics workflows on real hardware.

It has been revealed that simulation has been a cornerstone in medical imaging to address the data gap. However, in healthcare robotics until now, it's often been too slow, siloed, or difficult to translate into real-world systems.

NVIDIA Isaac for Healthcare, a developer framework for AI healthcare robotics, enables healthcare robotics developers in solving these challenges via offering integrated data collection, training, and evaluation pipelines that work across both simulation and hardware. Specifically, the Isaac for Healthcare v0.4 release provides healthcare developers with an end-to-end SO - ARM based starter workflow and the bring your own operating room tutorial. The SO-ARM starter workflow lowers the barrier for MedTech developers to experience the full workflow from simulation to train to deployment and start building and validating autonomous on real hardware right away.

In this post, we'll walk through the starter workflow and its technical implementation details to help you build a surgical assistant robot in less time than ever imaginable before.

The SO-ARM starter workflow introduces a upcoming way to explore surgical assistance tasks, and providing developers with a complete end-to-end pipeline for autonomous surgical assistance:.

This workflow gives developers a safe, repeatable environment to train and refine assistive skills before moving into the Operating Room.

The workflow implements a three-stage pipeline that integrates simulation and real hardware:.

Notably, over 93% of the data used for policy training was generated synthetically in simulation, underscoring the strength of simulation in bridging the robotic data gap.

Recent findings suggest that the workflow combines simulation and real-world data to address the fundamental challenge that training robots in the real world is expensive and limited, while pure simulation often fails to capture real-world complexities. The approach uses approximately 70 simulation episodes for diverse scenarios and environmental variations, combined with 10-20 real-world episodes for authenticity and grounding. This mixed training creates policies that generalize beyond either domain alone.

Notably, developers could run all the simulation, training and deployment (3 computers needed for physical AI) on one DGX Spark.

For users without physical SO-ARM101 hardware, the workflow provides keyboard-based teleoperation with the following joint controls:.

After collecting both simulation and real-world data, convert and combine datasets for training:.

The trained model processes natural language instructions such as "Prepare the scalpel for the surgeon" or "Hand me the forceps" and executes the corresponding robotic actions. With LeRobot latest release (0.4.0) you will be able to fine-tune Gr00t N1.5 natively in LeRobot!

Simulation is most powerful when it's part of a loop: collect → train → evaluate → deploy.

With v0.3, IsaacLab supports this full pipeline:.

This reduces time from experiment to deployment and makes sim2real a practical part of daily development.

Isaac for Healthcare SO-ARM Starter Workflow is available now. To get started:.

This is a fantastic deep dive into how Isaac’s Sim2Real pipeline is evolving medical robotics, the SO-ARM starter workflow is especially impressive for speeding up iteration in such a high-stakes domain.

Reading this alongside OpenForge’s Healthcare App Development: A Complete Guide -> recent piece on AI, UX, and compliance trends in healthcare app development really highlights how both hardware and software layers are converging around patient-centered intelligence.

Given that robotics workflows are increasingly handling critical procedures, how do you see design ethics and compliance considerations evolving when these AI-driven systems move from OR simulation to real surgical environments?

This is wonderful, but as a doctor having been in many ORs the real challenge becomes how a human assistant will know exactly what the surgeon wants next from building intuition with years of working alongside. Surgeons are very particular about their tools and the rhythm at which they expect the surgical team to work. Despite their reputation as grumps, they deeply value the humans in their team for that reason.

Sources indicate that this is amazing for what we can do with only a Spark which anybody could buy. But real OR use is many years away and so are the AI systems that will need to exist for that to happen.

This is amazing NVIDIA Isaac for Healthcare is redefining medical robotics! The seamless Sim2Real workflow & mixed data training make it easier than ever to build safe, intelligent surgical assistants. Truly the future of AI in healthcare.

Efficient Iterative Symmetrization algorithm for quantum computing and hadron applications

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (189 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.18091v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Efficient algorithms for the (anti)symmetrization of quantum registers are necessary for upcoming few- and many-body physics applications, from atomic to particle-physics scales. We propose a recursive algorithm (anti)symmetrizing the last particle added to memory, each time one is created or destroyed, respect to the rest of already (anti)symmetrized ones. Given a generalized Dicke state (GDS) of $(j-1)$ quantum registers, each assigned to a particle, the algorithm produces another GDS of $j$ registers (of $n_{qb}$ qubits each) using a mere $\mathcal{O}(j\log_2^2 j + j n_{qb})$ $\mathtt{CNOT}$ and single-qubit gates, and $3j+\lceil\log_2j\rceil+\mathcal{O}(\max(n_{qb},\log_2 j))$ clean auxiliary qubits. The (anti)symmetrizing operator constructed for this purpose depends on the quantum numbers of the additional particle being introduced or ``created''. The algorithm improves upon the construction presented in Appendix A of \cite{Galvez-Viruet:2024hry} by almost two powers of $j$ and is on par with the most efficient methods to date, while ideally suited for dynamical memory management with variable particle number. We exemplify its applicability with a small selection of problems from hadron physics which are expected to be addressable with upcoming quantum computers.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (270 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Model-family selection and recovery-gate design in generator-based noise tomography

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (270 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.11748v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Family selection in generator-model noise tomography is a hypothesis test whose shot floor has closed form under a purely coherent noise model, $N^{*}=\lambda_{\mathrm{req}}/(r_{\mathrm{b}} S)^{2}$: set by the absolute bias $r_{\mathrm{b}} S$, not the relative residual, and computable from a calibration alone. The same computation prices the recovery gates, fingerprint and Fisher information coming off the same map, so there is no design-independent verdict and no family-independent design optimum. Whether a design can move that price is structural: a bias confined to the block every design measures identically is design-blind, one that reaches the code blocks is repriced by a factor of sixty-eight---from a dominated design to the cheapest, not between two optima---and the two platforms studied here are its extremes. At the reference point the floor is $1.1\times10^{7}$ and $6.7\times10^{6}$ shots per component, the easy corner of the sampled working points, whose median floor is eighty-three times dearer in one direction and less than twice in the other; at the $10^{5}$ shots a run spends, the power equals the level and the residual reported is shot noise. The design problem is conditioning, not rank: across the sixty-four placements the rms varies by factors of $2.7$ and $3.9$, while the optimal gate count is flat at two to four. At five qubits the whole sample moves to $10^{9}$--$2\times10^{10}$ shots, a design spread of twenty-one against nine at three qubits; on a measured three-qubit register the floor is a requirement on systematic control before it is a shot count, and where that control is missing no budget supplies it.

#61804. Information--control limits for record-indistinguishable reset of a monitored qubit

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (276 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Information--control limits for record-indistinguishable reset of a monitored qubit

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (276 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.11393v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A qubit that is continuously monitored from the moment it is prepared in its excited state writes evidence of that preparation into its measurement record. We ask how much control is needed to reset such a qubit to its ground state while keeping its complete record statistically close to the record of an undriven ground-state qubit. The qubit is measured in $\sigma_z$ at rate $\Gamma_m$ with efficiency $\eta$ and has no relaxation. For feedback that acts causally on the record, distinguishability is the Kullback--Leibler divergence $D$ of the controlled record law from the reference law, and the control cost is the quadratic effort $J$, the integrated squared Rabi frequency. We prove that every open-loop drive leaves $D$ infinite and that every admissible control obeys $DJ\ge\Gamma_mU(\eta,D/\kappa_0)$, where $U$ is given by a one-parameter family of integrals and $\kappa_0=1-\ln2$. Our main result is the exact high-effort constant $\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\inf\{DJ/\Gamma_m: D\le\epsilon\}=K(\eta)$, where $K(\eta)=[\int_0^\pi\sqrt{2\eta(1+\cos\theta)^2+(1-\eta)\sin^2\theta}\,d\theta]^2$; an explicit sequence of two-phase feedback policies attains it. The first term of the integrand is the population evidence that the record receives while the qubit is rotated toward the ground state. The second is the price of the impurity created when the unrecorded part of the measurement dephases the coherence that the rotation needs; the record receives this evidence later, when the measurement repurifies the qubit. The global constant $c(\eta)=\inf DJ/\Gamma_m$ satisfies $K/2\le F_2\le c\le K$, where $F_2$ is again given by an integral; $c$ is known exactly at $\eta=1$ and in the limit $\eta\to0$. With any nonzero relaxation rate the unconstrained infimum of $DJ$ vanishes, so $c(\eta)$ is specific to the relaxation-free model.

#61800. Recovery gates as a resource in repetition-code process tomography: exhaustive gate-optimal designs for three, five and seven qubits

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (255 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Recovery gates as a resource in repetition-code process tomography: exhaustive gate-optimal designs for three, five and seven qubits

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (255 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.08310v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Repetition-code process tomography compares the logical channel of a code with a reference channel through a decoder almost always the standard minimum-weight one. We ask how many physical single-qubit Pauli gates that decoder needs when the measurement basis is fixed---the constraint that makes the count a resource. Exhaustive enumeration at $n=3$, $5$ and $7$, each rank decided in exact arithmetic, gives minima of $0$, $1$ and $5$ gates, against $6$, $10$ and $14$ for first-order decoding and $6$, $50$ and $308$ for full decoding. The count depends only on how many sites are corrected, not which, so the problem splits into a budget and a placement; the placement decides identifiability, and more sites is not monotonically better: at $n=7$ full decoding has rank $24$ of $27$, and under a calibration-residual floor the $n=3$ precision curve is U-shaped. The three-gate design is $9.0$ times more precise than the standard six-gate decoder at the median of $40$ working points and better at every one of them, by $1.8$ to $88$ times; with the placement fixed in advance the factor falls to $6.9$, or to $3.1$ for the pre-commitment never worse, both medians over the same $40$ points. Because the full advantage needs per-point placement, we also certify two placements in parallel: they lose no direction either sees and, wherever either is identifiable and the calibration floor permits, reach a $10$\,mrad target within twice the shots. The optimal designs are not covariant under chain reversal.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.08151v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Simulating strongly correlated electrons in molecules and materials remains a central goal for quantum computing. A promising strategy uses quantum processors to prepare trial wavefunctions that guide classical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC). However, the enormous computational cost of repeatedly processing quantum measurements has severely limited the practical scalability of this approach. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by compressing quantum measurement data into machine-learning models that efficiently provide the wavefunction overlaps needed by QMC. This accelerates quantum-classical QMC by orders of magnitude, enabling chemically accurate simulations on up to 40 qubits, more than doubling the scale of previous hardware demonstrations with comparable accuracy. We demonstrate our approach on hydrogen chains and strongly correlated iron-sulfur clusters using measurements from Google's Willow processor. By enabling efficient reuse of quantum-state information on the classical coprocessor, our framework addresses a fundamental bottleneck in hybrid quantum algorithms that will persist even into the fault-tolerant era.

#61785. Helium States Inspired by Quantum Photonics Circuit

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (237 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Helium States Inspired by Quantum Photonics Circuit

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (237 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.06448v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a four-mode Fock-state photonics implementation of the variational quantum deflation (VQD) algorithm to calculate the ground-state and excited-state energies for the neutral helium atom in a CAS(2,2) Subspace. Its CAS(2,2) electronic Hilbert space is encoded into a bosonic Fock-space representation and subsequently optimized using a continuous-variable quantum circuit. The circuit architecture under study is constructed of single-mode phase shifts, beam splitters, and cross-Kerr interactions. The variational circuit is initialized in the Fock state $\ket{1100}$ and its performance is benchmarked against exact diagonalization of the active-space configuration-interaction (CASCI) Hamiltonian. We also extend the method to optimize from the first to three excited states of the helium atom with the aid of the variational quantum deflation $(VQD)$ method in a CAS(2,2). We then investigate the performance of this circuit architecture as a basis for implementing the VQD method. In the ideal noiseless simulation setting, we see that the survival probability of the ground and the excited states within the target $CAS$ subspace is unity, because the total photon number and the photon number in the two spin sectors $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are preserved. We demonstrate that the proposed approach enables the determination of the ground and excited-state energies within the CAS(2,2) electronic Hilbert space using a continuous-variable quantum circuit and the variational quantum deflation ($VQD$) algorithm, while satisfying the orthogonality conditions with negligible errors.

Noise redistribution by stabilizer codes: an organizing view of concatenated three-qubit codes

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (264 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2610.31007v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We formulate stabilizer-code error correction as a code- and recovery-dependent transformation of the noise channel. For a fixed recovery map, syndrome projection produces a logical channel that is block diagonal with respect to the syndrome partition, whose diagonal Pauli weights are fixed by the code-induced error classes, with no physical Pauli twirl required. Concatenation is then iterated redistribution, with the dominant logical error guiding the next code. The bit-flip and phase-flip three-qubit codes with standard recoveries supply a closed-form benchmark, and logically inequivalent recoveries appear as a design degree of freedom for shaping the channel presented to the next decoder. For amplitude damping, the rules select $C_2(\hat\sigma_y)C_1(\hat\sigma_x)$ within this family: one level converts the damping into a nearly pure logical-$X$ channel at the price $f_1=1-3\gamma/4$, the second level suppresses that channel to $f_2=1-\frac94\gamma^2$, and the concatenated protocol overtakes the unencoded channel below $\gamma_c=0.2905$ ($f_c=0.8485$) under ideal encoding and recovery; with a per-gate error rate $\varepsilon$ the crossover survives only for $\varepsilon$ below about $5\times10^{-4}$, and then only inside a window of $\gamma$ that contracts as $\varepsilon$ grows. Across the $n$-qubit repetition family with odd $n$, the suppression order rises as $\gamma^{w+1}$ with $w=(n-1)/2$, while the gate budget grows as $n^L$. Correlated noise requires joint class statistics, whereas coherent noise retains intra-class coherences that make the same transformation usable in reverse as a tomographic fingerprint, whose local identifiability is established in a companion paper. The construction remains an analytic benchmark, not a universal prescription for an inner code beneath a surface code.

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Randomness Certification from Statistically Hiding Commitments

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (246 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2610.25518v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Randomness certification aims to guarantee that the output of an untrusted quantum device contains genuine randomness that remains unpredictable even given quantum side information held by an adversary. For a classical verifier interacting with a single quantum device, such a guarantee cannot rely on the physical separation underlying standard Bell tests and must instead follow from computational restrictions on the prover. Building on the framework of computational Bell inequalities, we distinguish classical and quantum virtual-input hiding, showing that the former suffices for proofs of quantumness, whereas the latter enables randomness certification against quantum side information. Our main technical contribution is to establish quantum virtual-input hiding for a commitment-based protocol derived from an earlier proof of quantumness (Morimae and Yamakawa, CRYPTO, 2024). We show that statistical hiding together with ordinary computational binding against quantum polynomial-time senders suffices, without requiring stronger quantum binding notions such as sum-binding or collapse-binding. This yields a randomness-certification protocol from post-quantum statistically hiding bit commitments. We give three instantiations. The NOVY commitment from any post-quantum one-way permutation yields randomness certification in the standard model with an inefficient classical verifier. Post-quantum trapdoor claw-free functions additionally provide trapdoor inversion, enabling an efficient classical verifier. In the quantum random-oracle model, a hash-based commitment yields randomness certification without additional computational assumptions, again with an inefficient verifier. These instantiations separate the cryptographic properties sufficient for randomness certification from the additional structure required for efficient verification within our commitment-based framework.

#61771. Efficient Quantum Monte Carlo through Cluster Expansions

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (211 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Efficient Quantum Monte Carlo through Cluster Expansions

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (211 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2610.03893v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The sign problem remains a major obstacle to extending the success of Monte Carlo methods to generic quantum many-body systems. A powerful alternative relies on cluster expansions, which provide convergent representations of free energies and related quantities, with applications ranging from tensor network contractions to quantum dynamics and circuits. Within their convergence regime, these expansions often yield deterministic polynomial-time algorithms. However, such methods require exhaustive enumeration of connected clusters, leading to a computational overhead of $(N\varepsilon^{-1})^{\mathcal{O}(\log\Delta)}$, where $N$ is the system size, $\varepsilon$ the desired precision, and $\Delta$ the interaction-graph degree. This becomes particularly severe in long-range systems, where $\Delta\equiv N$, resulting in quasi-polynomial runtimes. Here, we introduce a Markov chain algorithm that samples cluster expansions directly in the space of connected clusters, replacing deterministic enumeration by Monte Carlo sampling. Because sampling occurs in an abstract cluster space rather than a physical configuration space, the conventional exponential sign problem is absent within the convergence regime. For general polymer models, we establish an FPRAS with runtime $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(N^4\varepsilon^{-3})$. For quantum partition functions at temperatures $\beta\leq\beta_{\mathrm{sampling}}\equiv\mathcal{O}(1)$, this improves to $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(N^{3+1/D}\varepsilon^{-3})$, where $D$ is the lattice dimension. The framework applies to long-range quantum systems with interactions $\propto1/r^\alpha$, including $2$-local models with $\alpha>2D$.

A depolarizing choir sings in Gaussian harmony

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (158 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2609.39747v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the noise threshold for positive quantum capacity for the qubit depolarizing channel. We explore analytically the action of the qubit depolarizing channel on the symmetric subspaces of the input qubits, in the limit of asymptotically many uses of the channel. We observe the emergence of a bosonic Gaussian channel. Furthermore, the codes previously developed for the depolarizing channel can be translated to codes for the emergent Gaussian channel, and it is easier to further optimize these codes for the simpler emergent Gaussian channel. Translating these codes back to the depolarizing channel leads to extremely good input states for the coherent information of the depolarizing channel producing latest lower bounds on the noise threshold for positive capacity. In addition to improved lower bounds on the threshold, this newly found link between depolarizing noise and Gaussian channels offers a novel perspective contributing to our understanding of these symmetric codes.

#61754. Industry News: BEVCast: Path-Adaptive BEV for Efficient End-to-End Autonomous Driving

📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: BEVCast: Path-Adaptive BEV for Efficient End-to-End Autonomous Driving

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (254 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.08631v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Camera-based driving models build a dense bird's-eye-view (BEV) grid and spend the same computation on every cell of it, although the vehicle crosses only a few of those cells within the planning horizon. We present BEVCast, a two-stage BEV whose resolution adapts to the predicted driving path. A coarse pass encodes the whole scene on a grid of 4.096 m cells. A heat head trained on the recorded path assigns a heat to every coarse cell and the cells with the highest heat are refined into 1.024 m cells under a fixed budget. The remaining cells keep their coarse resolution, so the trajectory head reads a mixed-resolution BEV that still covers the entire scene and needs neither an HD map nor a navigation command. Against a full grid of 1.024 m cells with the same architecture and training recipe, BEVCast at a 10% refinement budget encodes 28% of the BEV queries and needs 66% of the BEV encoder time at batch size 1. On nuScenes its mean displacement error is 1.078 m against 1.149 m and its drivable area violation rate is 1.46% against 2.29%. On NAVSIM navtest its mean displacement error is 0.577 m against 0.598 m and its extended predictive driver model score is 82.51 against 81.28. Next to published planners BEVCast reaches a comparable error on both benchmarks without a navigation command. The resolution of a driving BEV can therefore follow the task instead of the grid.

#61749. Consensus Within, Competition Between: Decentralized LLM Teams for Perimeter Defense

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (228 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Consensus Within, Competition Between: Decentralized LLM Teams for Perimeter Defense

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (228 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2610.41044v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The use of large language models (LLMs) to coordinate multi-agent teams raises a fundamental architectural question: whether task allocation should be centralized in a single LLM controller or distributed across autonomous LLM agents, particularly when communication is unreliable. In a deliberately simplified perimeter-defense simulation against LLM-controlled intruders, we compared a central commander, an auction-based consensus team and independent agents under five network conditions. Breach rates were 15% for the consensus team, 32% for the commander and 29% for independent agents. Burst message loss, falsified reports and limited radio range raised the commander's breach rate by 10 to 18 percentage points (pp), whereas the consensus team's changed by at most 5. In the consensus team, giving a low-cost LLM more authority over the bid computation raised its breach rate by 38 pp. With birds and civilian drones in airspace, we added an image for each to the input text state. Only the near-frontier model treated them apart from intruders. Intruders disguised as existing taxidermy bird drones were mistaken for birds by both low-cost and near-frontier LLMs, being dropped from pursuit in 59-61% of near-frontier decisions (1-16% before). However, a one-sentence forewarning in the prompt lowered it to 0-25%. We find that the LLM team with a dedicated external conflict-resolution protocol had the fewest breaches. The code is available at https://github.com/the-kas-lab/consensus-within-competition-between.

#61735. Nonequilibrium energy transport and fluctuations in two-photon-driven nonlinear quantum optical systems

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (207 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Nonequilibrium energy transport and fluctuations in two-photon-driven nonlinear quantum optical systems

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (207 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2609.23651v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding nonequilibrium transport and fluctuations under a parametric drive in nonlinear quantum optical systems is challenging. Here, we formulate a driven quantum master equation in the rotating frame combined with full counting statistics, retaining the drive-induced frequency shifts in the system-reservoir interactions and providing a unified description of drive-assisted incoherent transitions based on the rotated system dressed-basis. Applied to a Kerr resonator and a nonlinear Jaynes-Cummings model, the approach reveals pronounced multiphoton-resonant enhancement of the drive input energy current, with significant high peaks under two-photon driving compared to the single-photon case. The two-photon resonance relations are analytically obtained. Resonance structure in the nonlinear Jaynes-Cummings model nonlinearly relies on qubit-photon couplings, with additional dressed-state branches. A low-energy-state approximation attributes the resonant current enhancement to dressed-state hybridization and efficient activation of incoherent energy exchange processes. Beyond the average current, two-photon-driving induced energy exchange picture near resonance also substantially modifies the second-order current fluctuation and higher-order current cumulant, while increasing the time-normalized signal-to-noise ratio. Adding two-photon loss introduces extra incoherent photon-pair exchange pathways and further reshapes the current and its fluctuations. We hope these results may deepen interpretation of photon driving and quantum dissipation cooperatively governing nonequilibrium energy transport and fluctuations.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (281 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Latent Projection for Latent Planning

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (281 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2610.26979v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Latent world models let an agent plan in latent space. The planner searches for an action sequence that minimizes a cost, and that cost is often the $\ell_2$ distance between the predicted terminal latent and the goal latent. The latent, however, is partly noise: the regularizer that prevents collapse during world model training promotes variance in the directions carrying no signal. We show that the same regularizer also supplies the structure to prune that noise in the latent. SIGReg drives the latent marginal to a standard Gaussian at every step, and assuming further that the latent sequence is a Gauss-Markov process, the transition is linear with its covariance pinned by the map itself, $z' \mid z \sim N(Az,\, I - AA^\top)$. Fitting the state dynamics $A$ therefore yields the covariance at no additional cost, and in its eigenbasis each latent direction carries its own uncertainty. Furthermore, constraining $A$ to be a normal matrix fixes that basis across timesteps, so one eigenbasis measures the uncertainty over an arbitrary number of steps and serves as a stable basis to compute the planning cost on. We then restrict the $\ell_2$ cost to the $k$-dimensional subspace the state dynamics carry forward with the least uncertainty. The correction is post hoc: the encoder, the predictor, the rollout, and the planner are all left untouched, and only a single constrained matrix, $A$, is fit. We evaluate across six environments and show large gains on the 2D navigation tasks, TwoRoom and PointMaze, raising success rate over the plain $\ell_2$ cost by up to $+54.7$ points under a harder planning setting. Code is available at https://github.com/yjang43/lp2.

Breaking: Exact Replica-Sector Hierarchy of Multi-Resolvent Spectral-Weight Fluctuations in Random Free Fermions

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (209 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

In a recent development, arXiv:2609.17037v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The one-point ETH envelope fixes the smooth part of a spectral density but not how the spectral weight of an eigenstate is distributed across channels; its higher-order correlations are joint fluctuations of those weights and are carried by connected products of channel resolvents. In random free fermions every channel overlap is a squared Slater minor of a Haar-orthogonal one-body eigenvector matrix, and the multi-resolvent hierarchy has an exact microscopic realization there. The $r$-resolvent moment admits a decomposition into finitely many overlap sectors whose values are fixed by the channel and eigenstate overlap patterns and whose weights are exact finite-$N$ orthogonal Weingarten functions: the sector theorem holds at arbitrary finite multiplicity, it is realized in full at $r=3$ ($k=2,3,4$) and through exact sector slices at $r=4,5$, and the sector moments lift to connected resolvent cumulants and to the irreducible Feshbach self-energy vertices, whose deep plane begins at the order $z^{-(3r-2)}$. At $r=2$ this structure reproduces and completes an exact benchmark in which a flat envelope coexists with a non-Porter--Thomas intensity hierarchy and closes the two-resolvent covariance, and under interaction it separates into a deep plane fixed by Hamiltonian channel moments and a bulk that requires eigenstate-resolved information.

#61715. HAVANA: A Hierarchical Video-Action Model for Vision-Language Navigation

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (181 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

HAVANA: A Hierarchical Video-Action Model for Vision-Language Navigation

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (181 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2610.24122v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires long-horizon instruction-consistent planning and short-horizon path planning grounded in the right now observed geometry. Anticipating how future observations evolve along the instructed route provides predictive guidance beyond the current field of view, motivating video-action models (VAMs) that learn representations of future visual states. However, many existing VAMs couple future visual prediction with action generation during inference, despite their distinct temporal requirements: instruction-conditioned route guidance can be reused across multiple control steps, whereas local trajectories must continuously adapt to fresh observations. To bridge this gap, we introduce HAVANA, a dual-system VAM that decouples predictive reasoning from reactive local planning. A slow system produces a compact language-conditioned latent plan from observation history, while a fast system combines the latest plan with the current observation to generate local trajectories. Their asynchronous execution enables rapid adaptation without repeated future prediction, and no future video is generated during inference. Experiments on OmniNavBench demonstrate state-of-the-art navigation performance over prior baselines, while zero-shot real-world deployments further show robust generalization to unseen environments.

#61711. Industry News: CtRoFlow: Monocular Camera-to-Robot Pose Estimation via Conditioned 3D Flow Matching

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (174 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: CtRoFlow: Monocular Camera-to-Robot Pose Estimation via Conditioned 3D Flow Matching

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (174 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2610.21086v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Camera-to-robot pose estimation from a monocular image is significant for vision-based robot navigation and control. Existing camera-to-robot pose estimation methods either rely on time-consuming iterative rendering, PnP based on predicted 2D keypoints with limited robustness or 3D registration which suffers from monocular scale ambiguity and complex training configuration. In this work, we propose CtRoFlow, a flow matching-based framework for camera-to-robot pose estimation. From the predicted 2D heatmaps, we propose a Keypoint-centered Feature Extractor (KFE) to obtain positional features along with contextual representations from keypoints-centered multi-scale patches. Moreover, we introduce Graph-guided Condition Generator (GCG), which generates condition for flow matching based on correlation among keypoints. Besides, we introduce Bone Length Loss and Ray-based Loss for decoupled training and scale consistency, with joint-wise weighting to mitigate varied prediction difficulty across joints. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods for pose estimation across different types of robots with multiple cameras, as well as for zero-shot cross-scene robot pose estimation. Code will be available upon acceptance.

#61703. VGGT-VLA-World: Intent-Conditioned 3D World Evolution for Autonomous Driving

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (194 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

VGGT-VLA-World: Intent-Conditioned 3D World Evolution for Autonomous Driving

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (194 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2610.11161v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: VGGT provides a strong foundation for geometry-centric world models by recovering unified 3D scene geometry from visual observations. Although recent extensions enable temporal 3D prediction, their future evolution remains weakly conditioned on driving intentions and actions, limiting their ability to model alternative action-dependent futures. We propose \textbf{VGGTWorld-VLA}, an intention-conditioned extension of VGGT-World for controllable 3D world evolution in autonomous driving. First, we introduce an action--semantic conditioning mechanism that injects complementary driving semantics and ego-motion representations into the future-token stream, enabling different future geometry predictions for the same observed scene under alternative ego actions. Second, we develop a geometry--language--action bridge that adapts historical geometry, VLA semantic features, and maneuver and trajectory representations for joint conditioning of future geometry prediction. We evaluate future geometry prediction on NAVSIM, with ablation studies examining the contributions of semantic and action conditioning. Compared with baseline, our method reduces future-depth RMSE by 13.7\% and improves $\delta_1$ by 4.11 percentage points on NAVSIM motion subset. Controlled action-input interventions further show that the model uses the supplied action information. These results support semantic and action conditioning for controllable VGGT-based world prediction in autonomous driving.

Industry News: Current statistics for quantum transport along a bosonic tight-binding chain connected to Markovian reservoirs

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (99 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2609.11741v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study quantum transport of non-interacting particles in a bosonic tight-binding chain coupled to Markovian reservoirs at its boundaries. Using the analytic solution in the form of an anti-normally ordered quantum characteristic function, we obtain exact probability distribution functions for the current on each bond in the chain, as well as the inter-bond current correlation functions. We extend the analysis to tight-binding chains subject to uniform on-site phase damping. In the phasedamped case, we find that a Gaussian approximation for the quantum characteristic functions predicts current fluctuations with good accuracy.

#61695. Proof-of-principle long-distance Sagnac twin-field quantum key distribution network

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (178 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Proof-of-principle long-distance Sagnac twin-field quantum key distribution network

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (178 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2609.04447v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Twin-field (TF) quantum key distribution (QKD) offers a promising approach to long-distance QKD networks due to its superior performance over large channel losses. Due to specialized hardware requirements, nearly all long-distance TFQKD demonstrations have only two users exchanging keys, rather than a network with three or more users. In this work, we experimentally demonstrate a proof-of-principle three-user-pair Sagnac TFQKD network spanning 127-km using single-photon avalanche detectors without any active phase stabilization or postcompensation. We implement efficient procedures for maintaining polarization stability and circumventing Rayleigh backscattering noise to achieve a stable Sagnac interference visibility of $93\pm1$ % over one hour. Using measured data for the signal basis and simulated data for the decoy basis, an asymptotic secure key rate of $1.398\times10^{-5}$ bits per pulse is achieved over an asymmetric communication channel with 102-km fiber and 45-dB overall loss. To our knowledge, this is the first TFQKD network without active phase stabilization or postcompensation achieved over long fibers. Our results represent a highly practical and cost-effective approach to long-distance QKD networks.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (194 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

World-Model Gradient Refinement in CEM: An Empirical Study

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (194 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2610.00921v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The cross-entropy method (CEM) uses world-model predictions both to select action sequences and to determine where to sample next. We isolate the effect of an early revision by replacing only the first model-ranked elite set with environment-ranked elites. This fixed-state intervention lowers the selected sequence's realised tracking cost in all 12 Walker/Cheetah task-seed units. We then study short gradient updates to top-ranked candidates as a way to improve search under the model's own objective. Across 52 frozen TD-MPC2 checkpoints from 32 tasks, we compare refinement with additional CEM sampling at the same planning budget, tuning both planners' initial proposal widths. We fix the groups before this comparison using an exploratory model-only diagnostic. Refinement gains 67.8 return points on average (95\% CI [31.9, 103.6]) on ten checkpoints with large model-predicted improvements, and 0.2 ([$-2.9$, 3.4]) on the remaining 42. The diagnostic's rank test on 24 fresh checkpoints fails, so the association does not establish a predictive rule. Offline analyses show local benefits on some tasks and positive estimates for both proposal refitting and final selection. End-of-search polishing also helps, leaving the need for repeated refitting unresolved.

#61672. ActionUNet: Improving Robustness of VLA Models with Efficient Multi-scale Fine-tuning

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

ActionUNet: Improving Robustness of VLA Models with Efficient Multi-scale Fine-tuning

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (224 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2609.34982v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown great promise for robotic manipulation by mapping multi-modal semantics to physical actions. However, this mapping inherently struggles to align these coarse-grained semantics with fine-grained temporal execution. It leaves VLA models with limited generalization and insufficient robustness in cluttered environments. To overcome this issue, we propose ActionUNet, an efficient multi-scale fine-tuning framework that enhances pre-trained VLA models with minimal computational cost. ActionUNet first constructs a lightweight temporal U-Net within the temporal-aligned action feature space to fuse hierarchical structural priors, effectively bridging the scale gap between semantics and temporal executions. Recognizing that multi-scale modeling can disrupt microscopic temporal continuity and cause mechanical oscillations, ActionUNet then employs a conditional SIREN as a continuous action decoder. Equipped with explicit second-order smoothness constraints, this decoder guarantees temporal continuity and reduces high-frequency motion jitter. By smoothing temporal discontinuities from multi-scale fusion, this continuous formulation reduces mechanical execution failures while preserving the base VLA model's generalization and manipulation robustness. Extensive experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks, together with real-world hard evaluations, demonstrate that ActionUNet significantly improves {\pi}0.5 success rates by absolute 9.8%, 6.1%, and 11.4%, respectively, while also generalizing to the regression-based OpenVLA-OFT backbone, highlighting its effectiveness and efficiency as a fine-tuning strategy. Code and implementation details are available at https://github.com/Di-Zhu123/ActionUNet.
